pronunciation.approximation: SEH-shaht; the middle consonant is the aleph (ꜣ), not the ayin.
pronunciation.note: Sšꜣt is conventionally vocalized "Seshat"; the doubled s of older "Sesheta" spellings and the final t mark her as the female counterpart of Thoth in both function and grammar. The ꜣ (Gardiner G1, the vulture) is the glottal stop the restoration keeps, where older books printed a plain "a."

domains.title: The Lady of the Record
domains.subtitle: Writing, Measurement, and the Stretching of the Cord
domains.lead: Sšꜣt is Egypt's goddess of everything written down: founder of libraries, keeper of the royal annals, and the king's partner in the "stretching of the cord" — the rite that laid every temple's axis on the stars. Seven-pointed star above her head, palm-rib in her hand, she is precision itself.

cards.name: The Annals
cards.desc: She writes the king's regnal years and victories — the memory of Egypt in her hand.

cards.name: The Seven-Pointed Star
cards.desc: Her emblem, read as star, rosette, or inverted horns — scholarship still debates it; she has not told.

cards.name: Stretching the Cord
cards.desc: The foundation rite: she and the king stretch the line that fixes the temple on the heavens.

cards.name: The Palm-Rib
cards.desc: Her notched tally-stick: the years themselves, carved in wood that outlasts reigns.

symbols.name: The seven-pointed star

mythology.lead: Sšꜣt rarely stars in myth-narrative; she is present at the moments that matter — foundations, jubilees, coronations — because those moments are made of measurement and record, and she is both.

myths.title: Pedj-Shes
myths.text: The pedj-shes, ‘stretching of the cord’, opens every temple: at night, sighting on the stars, the king and Sšꜣt stretch a cord between stakes to fix the building’s axis — she the goddess of measurement, he the builder under her hand. The reliefs show the rite exactly and never change it: Seti I’s temple at Abydos (Dynasty 19), Hatshepsut’s foundation works, and the Ptolemaic temples of Edfu and Dendera a thousand years later all show the same two figures facing each other, mallet and pole in hand, the captions declaiming the grip on peg and cord. A temple in Egypt is not built; it is measured into alignment with the turning sky, and the measurer is a goddess. The rite’s survival across three millennia makes it the longest continuously documented foundation ceremony on earth — and its modern descendant is the theodolite.

myths.title: The Notches of Time
myths.text: At the jubilee, the sed-festival, she offers the king the palm-rib notched with countless years — ‘I give you years as numerous as those of Ra.’ She is the accountant of eternity: regnal years, the biennial cattle-census, the flood’s height, the captured spoil — all are inscribed by her. The surviving royal annals, above all the Palermo Stone (Dynasty 5), are her liturgy made stone: reign by reign, the stone records the cattle-count, the gold-count, the Nile’s rise, and the king’s works. What she writes, the king truly possesses; what she omits, history loses. The doctrine is the archive’s own: a deed exists, in Egyptian theology, only once it has been counted and written down — and the official who makes it exist, the oldest professional in government, is a goddess.

myths.title: Mistress of the House of Books
myths.text: Her titles are institutional: ‘foremost of the house of books’, the temple library, and ‘mistress of the house of architects’ — the two rooms where Egyptian knowledge actually lived. Medical, ritual, and astronomical texts were said to come from her chamber, and the scribal colophons invoke her world of measured knowledge even where her name is not written. When later ages imagined a single goddess of wisdom, Sšꜣt had already held the office for three thousand years. Her eventual pairing with Djehuty (Thoth) is later theology’s way of marrying the two halves of sacred knowledge: his writing and her measurement, his moon and her star. The Greeks, finding no clean equivalent, simply transliterated her name — a rare compliment — and left the office stubbornly Egyptian.

myths.title: With Thoth
myths.text: Later theology pairs her with Djehuty, Thoth — as daughter or consort, the sources vary — the moon-scribe and the star-measurer, the two halves of sacred knowledge walking hand in hand through the Late and Ptolemaic temples. She is, in the pairing, the ground of his writing: the measurement that gives knowledge its ground, the record that gives it its memory, the star above the moon. The pairing does what theology does best — it takes two offices, archiving and inscribing, and binds them into a marriage so that no temple can hold one without the other. Temples that measured without writing forgot why they were aligned; temples that wrote without measuring wrote fiction. Sšꜣt is the argument that truth needs both, and the argument is cast in the one form the Egyptians trusted to last: not a treatise, but a goddess, carved in the doorway of every great temple.

myths.title: The Count of All Things
myths.text: The annals of Egypt — the Palermo Stone and its lost siblings — are her liturgy made stone: reign by reign, the stone records the biennial cattle-count, the gold-count, the flood’s height, and the king’s works, each entry a notch in the national memory. Conquest reliefs show her at the king’s elbow with the palm-rib while the scribes tally severed hands and herds: the king’s victory is not complete, the theology insists, until it has been counted. When a king boasts of enumerating his spoils, she is the enumeration. The Egyptians called such records ‘what Seshat writes’ — and the phrase is the first doctrine of the archive in world history: power follows from record, and the surveyor precedes the sovereign. Every modern census, ledger, and land registry is a secular echo of the goddess who stood at the founding of the first one.

lore.syncretism: The Greeks found no clean equivalent — she sits between the Muses, Mnemosyne, and Athena Polias' architectural side — and mostly left her untranslated, a mark of how specifically Egyptian the office was. In Hermetic literature her functions migrate toward Thoth-Hermes Trismegistus: the great scribe absorbs his lady's archive. Modern revivals quietly restored her: she is the unofficial patroness of librarians, archivists, and surveyors who know her seven-pointed star.
lore.culturalLegacy: She embodies an idea the modern world runs on: that power follows from record — the survey, the ledger, the archive. Egyptologists cite her rite in every study of temple alignment (the "stretching of the cord" is the founding document of archaeoastronomy), and her palm-rib is the ancestor of every tally, census, and database. Wherever a foundation stone is laid by measure rather than by guess, her cord is still stretched.
lore.extendedMeditation: Sšꜣt is the goddess of "write it down." Civilization begins, in her liturgy, not with fire or the wheel but with the cord and the notch: measure the ground, record the year. She asks of every age drowning in information the only question that matters: what, of all this, have you measured truly enough to keep?

lore.archaeology: Her iconography is remarkably consistent across three millennia: leopard-skin robe, seven-pointed emblem on a double horizontal bar, palm-rib in hand. The finest foundation reliefs — Seti I at Abydos, Hatshepsut's foundation deposits, Edfu and Dendera's Ptolemaic versions — show the cord-stretching in identical form, a ritual grammar unchanged from Old Kingdom to Rome. Foundation deposits under real temples (model tools, plaques, the cord's physical traces) confirm the rite was performed, not just pictured.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written with the reed-leaf sš (M22, the sign that also gives the word for "scribe" and "writing"), followed by ꜣ and the feminine t. Her very name is built from the hieroglyph for writing — she is the only goddess whose spelling is her job description.
